# CISA, the Secure Software Development Attestation Form

**Source:** Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US Department of Homeland Security, "Secure Software Development Attestation Form Instructions", containing the Secure Software Development Attestation Form, Version 1.0. OMB Control #: 1670-0052, expiration date 03/31/2027. A 10-page fillable PDF; no issue date is printed (PDF metadata: created 2024-04-23). The document states no copyright or licence terms; recorded by the operator as a US federal government work. Scope: open.
**Structure:** Privacy Act Statement (p. 1); purpose, scope and submission instructions (pp. 2–3); completing and signing the form, third-party assessment, and what happens without an attestation (pp. 3–4); the form itself, Sections I–III (pp. 5–7); burden statement (p. 8); an appendix mapping each requirement to E.O. 14028 subsections and to SSDF practices and tasks (pp. 9–10).

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The form is how a software producer attests that the software it produces is developed in conformity with specified secure software development practices; its stated purpose is to give the Federal Government assurances that software used by agencies is securely developed (pp. 1–2). Its background sets out, in turn, FISMA, which authorises the OMB Director to promulgate information security standards; E.O. 14028, which required NIST guidance on practices that enhance software supply chain security and the OMB Director to ensure agencies comply with it; and OMB M-22-18 as amended by M-23-16, under which an agency may use covered software only if its producer has first attested to compliance with practices drawn from the SSDF, NIST SP 800-218 (pp. 1–2, 6). The form says it fulfils the minimum requirements OMB set in M-22-18 as amended (p. 4).

In Section III the signer attests that, to the best of their knowledge, the producer presently makes consistent use of four practices derived from the SSDF, and that the producer will notify every agency it submitted the form to if and when it stops (pp. 6–7). The CEO or a designee who is an employee with authority to bind the corporation signs. A third-party assessment by a qualifying 3PAO can stand in for the signature, and an agency that cannot obtain a completed self-attestation may still decide to use the software if the producer identifies the practices it cannot attest to, documents mitigating practices and submits a POA&M; the agency is then responsible for requesting an extension or waiver from OMB (p. 4).

## Authority and Purpose

The Privacy Act Statement is unique to DHS; every agency using the common form will need to provide its own (p. 1). It gives the authority for the collection as 44 U.S.C. § 3554, E.O. 14028 and M-22-18 as amended by M-23-16, says the form collects contact information from the vendor employees who make the attestation, and names two consequences: failing to provide requested information may lead the agency to stop using the software, and willfully providing false or misleading information may violate 18 U.S.C. § 1001, a criminal statute (p. 1).

FISMA requires each agency to protect information collected or maintained by it or on its behalf and information systems used or operated by it or on its behalf, and FISMA and other provisions of Federal law authorise the OMB Director to promulgate information security standards, including to ensure compliance with NIST standards (p. 2). E.O. 14028 required NIST guidance identifying practices that enhance software supply chain security; the SSDF (SP 800-218) and the NIST Software Supply Chain Security Guidance, taken together as "NIST Guidance", include a set of practices that create the foundation for developing secure software (p. 2). OMB issued M-22-18 on September 14, 2022, and updated it through M-23-16 on June 9, 2023 (p. 2). The form identifies the minimum requirements a producer must meet, and attest to meeting, before covered software may be used by Federal agencies (p. 2).

## Which Software Needs an Attestation

Self-attestation is required if any of three conditions holds: the software was developed after September 14, 2022; it was developed before that date but modified by major version changes after it (the form's example is a version number going from 2.5 to 3.0 under Major.Minor.Patch); or the producer delivers continuous changes to the code, as with software-as-a-service or continuous delivery/continuous deployment (pp. 2–3). Four categories are out of scope and need no attestation: software developed by Federal agencies; open-source software freely and directly obtained by a Federal agency; third-party open source and proprietary components incorporated into the software end product the agency uses; and software that is freely obtained and publicly available (p. 3). Section I repeats them as what the form does not cover, applied to the specified software or any of its components (p. 5).

Producers who use third-party components must attest that they have taken the specific steps in Section III to minimise the risks of relying on those components (p. 3), and a note in Section I says that in signing, software producers attest to adhering to the Section III practices for code developed by the producer (p. 5). Footnote 4 makes attestations binding for future versions of the named product until the producer notifies the agencies it submitted to that its practices no longer conform to the attestation's required elements (p. 5).

## Completing, Submitting and Signing

Agencies may give agency-specific instructions outside the common form, conformance to agency-specific requirements may be attached as an addendum, and agencies handle any Paperwork Reduction Act requirements for those additions (p. 3). The form is submitted online at softwaresecurity.cisa.gov or, if the producer cannot use the online form, emailed as a PDF to the agency, named in the pattern `[Software Producer]_[Product]_[Version]_[Attestation Date]` (example `Acme_SecuritySuite_4.6.2.1_20230124`) (p. 3). All fields must be appropriately completed, and incomplete forms will not be accepted (p. 3).

Section I records the attestation's status (new, following an extension or waiver, or revised), its type (company-wide, an individual product, or multiple products or specific product versions) and, for products, each name, version number and release/publish date, with extra pages allowed (p. 5). Section II records the producer's company details and a primary contact, which may be an individual, role or group, with an email address that may be a distribution list (pp. 5–6).

The form must be signed by the producer's CEO or a designee who is an employee with authority to bind the corporation; by signing, that person attests that the software is developed in conformity with the practices in the form, and an agency may use the software once it has received an appropriately signed copy (p. 4).

## Alternatives: Third-Party Assessment, POA&M, Extension or Waiver

A producer may instead demonstrate conformance by submitting a third-party assessment (p. 4). The assessor must be a 3PAO that is FedRAMP certified or approved in writing by an appropriate agency official; it must use relevant NIST Guidance that includes all the form's elements as its assessment baseline; the producer checks the box in Section III and attaches the assessment, and need not sign; and the agency must take appropriate steps to keep the assessment from being posted publicly by the vendor or the agency (p. 4). The Section III statement says the 3PAO has evaluated "our conformance to all elements in this form" [V] and that the assessment is attached (p. 7).

If an agency cannot obtain a completed self-attestation, it may still decide to use the software if the producer identifies the practices it cannot attest to, documents the practices it has in place to mitigate the associated risks, and submits a plan of actions and milestones (POA&M) to the agency (p. 4). When no attestation is provided, per OMB guidance, the agency is responsible for requesting an extension or waiver from OMB for continued use; Section I has a status checkbox for an attestation following an extension or waiver (pp. 4–5). The form and its instructions are subject to change (p. 4).

## The Attestation Requirements (Section III)

The signer attests, on the company's behalf and to the best of their knowledge, that the producer "presently makes consistent use of the following practices, derived from the secure software development framework (SSDF)" [V], in developing the software identified in Section I (p. 6). The requirements, in the form's words (pp. 6–7):

- **1.** "The software is developed and built in secure environments. Those environments are secured by the following actions, at a minimum:" [V]
- **1a.** "Separating and protecting each environment involved in developing and building software;" [V]
- **1b.** "Regularly logging, monitoring, and auditing trust relationships used for authorization and access:" [V], (i) "to any software development and build environments" [V] and (ii) "among components within each environment" [V]
- **1c.** "Enforcing multi-factor authentication and conditional access across the environments relevant to developing and building software in a manner that minimizes security risk;" [V]
- **1d.** "Taking consistent and reasonable steps to document, as well as minimize use or inclusion of software products that create undue risk within the environments used to develop and build software;" [V]
- **1e.** "Encrypting sensitive data, such as credentials, to the extent practicable and based on risk;" [V]
- **1f.** "Implementing defensive cybersecurity practices, including continuous monitoring of operations and alerts and, as necessary, responding to suspected and confirmed cyber incidents;" [V]
- **2.** "The software producer makes a good-faith effort to maintain trusted source code supply chains by employing automated tools or comparable processes to address the security of internal code and third-party components and manage related vulnerabilities;" [V]
- **3.** "The software producer maintains provenance for internal code and third-party components incorporated into the software to the greatest extent feasible;" [V]
- **4.** "The software producer employs automated tools or comparable processes that check for security vulnerabilities. In addition:" [V]
- **4a.** "The software producer operates these processes on an ongoing basis and prior to product, version, or update releases;" [V]
- **4b.** "The software producer has a policy or process to address discovered security vulnerabilities prior to product release; and" [V]
- **4c.** "The software producer operates a vulnerability disclosure program and accepts, reviews, and addresses disclosed software vulnerabilities in a timely fashion and according to any timelines specified in the vulnerability disclosure program or applicable policies." [V]
- **Further attestation.** "I further attest that the software producer will notify any agency to which it has submitted this form if and when the producer ceases to make consistent use of the practices identified above in developing the software." [V]

The signature block is for the CEO or designee with authority to bind the corporation, with date, name and title; "OR" the third-party-assessment statement; then a list of attachments (p. 7). The PDF's form fields give the further attestation and the third-party statement a checkbox each, and none to practices 1–4 or their sub-items (field list, pp. 6–7). The appendix restates practice 4 with "employed" for "employs" (p. 10).

## The Appendix Mapping

The minimum requirements address E.O. 14028 subsection (4)(e), and the mapping to SSDF practices and tasks is given for reference purposes (p. 9). As printed (pp. 9–10; row 2 prints four codes without the dot):

| Requirement | E.O. 14028 subsection | Related SSDF practices and tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4e(i) | [See rows below] |
| 1a | 4e(i)(A) | PO.5.1 |
| 1b | 4e(i)(B) | PO.5.1 |
| 1c | 4e(i)(C) | PO.5.1, PO.5.2 |
| 1d | 4e(i)(D) | PO.5.1 |
| 1e | 4e(i)(E) | PO.5.2 |
| 1f | 4e(i)(F) | PO.3.2, PO.3.3, PO.5.1, PO.5.2 |
| 2 | 4e(iii) | PO 1.1, PO.3.1, PO.3.2, PO.5.1, PO.5.2, PS.1.1, PS.2.1, PS.3.1, PW.4.1, PW.4.4, PW 7.1, PW 8.1, RV 1.1 |
| 3 | 4e(vi) | PO.1.3, PO.3.2, PO.5.1, PO.5.2, PS.3.1, PS.3.2, PW.4.1, PW.4.4, RV.1.1, RV.1.2 |
| 4, 4a–4c (one cell) | 4e(iv) | PO.4.1, PO.4.2, PS.1.1, PW.2.1, PW.4.4, PW.5.1, PW.6.1, PW.6.2, PW.7.1, PW.7.2, PW.8.2, PW.9.1, PW.9.2, RV.1.1, RV.1.2, RV.1.3, RV.2.1, RV.2.2, RV.3.3 |

The further attestation has no row (pp. 9–10). The form cites SSDF practices and tasks by code only.

## Key Statistics

- OMB Control #: 1670-0052; expiration date 03/31/2027 (every page; p. 8).
- Form Version 1.0 (p. 5).
- Estimated burden: 3 hours and 20 minutes per response (p. 8).
- M-22-18 issued September 14, 2022; M-23-16 update June 9, 2023 (p. 2).
- Section III: practices 1–4, with 1a–1f and 4a–4c, plus the further attestation to notify (pp. 6–7).

## Key Connections

- E.O. 14028, "Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity": an authority for the collection; Section 4(e) required the NIST guidance; subsection (4)(e) puts forth the requirements the minimum requirements address (pp. 1–2, 9–10).
- OMB M-22-18 as amended by M-23-16: the requirement to attest, its scope, and the minimum requirements the form fulfils (pp. 1–4).
- NIST SSDF, SP 800-218: the framework the practices derive from, cited by code in the appendix (pp. 2, 6, 9–10).
- NIST Software Supply Chain Security Guidance: with the SSDF, "NIST Guidance", which a 3PAO must use as part of its assessment baseline (pp. 2, 4, 7).
- FISMA; 44 U.S.C. § 3554; 18 U.S.C. § 1001; DHS/ALL-002 (73 FR 71659); FedRAMP; the Paperwork Reduction Act; OMB guidance on extensions and waivers (pp. 1–4).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

None. The form states requirements and procedures and argues against no position.
